title: Optimization of Deep Neural Networks for Multivariate Data: Systematic Review and Critical Analysis of Methods, Hyperparameters, and Performance (2015–2026)
abstract: Optimizing deep neural networks for multivariate data remains difficult: features are high-dimensional, correlated, and heterogeneous, and no existing review connects optimization strategy, hyperparameter choice, and data type into a single picture. We address this gap through a Systematic Mapping Study of 107 articles published between 2015 and 2026, drawn from Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Web of Science, screened with a PRISMA-style protocol and clear inclusion/exclusion criteria. Metaheuristics dominate the corpus (49% of studies), followed by hybrid approaches (24%) and learning-based methods (18%). We catalogued over 50 optimization algorithms and grouped them into a five-level taxonomy. The learning rate turned out to be the single most influential hyperparameter, cited in nearly 40% of cases, well ahead of network depth, width, or batch size. Multivariate time series was studied far more than any other data type, making up close to half of the reviewed publications; medical/biometric and financial applications came next. Most studies still report classification metrics such as accuracy and F1-score, even for time series problems where a regression measure would often fit better. A co-occurrence analysis ties optimization families to application domains, and both a chi-square test and a Kendall rank correlation suggest these patterns are not simply due to chance. Four problems keep coming up across the literature: high computational cost, overfitting, a shortage of labeled data, and limited interpretability. These gaps shape our recommendations, which include wider use of auto-tuning methods, fairer evaluation metrics, and more attention to under-studied domains such as agriculture and industrial Internet of Things. title: Testing quantum gravity with cold atoms: A quantum-information method
abstract: We investigate the interface between quantum mechanics and gravity employing techniques from quantum information theory. The focus is primarily on investigating the gravitationally mediated entanglement (measured here by the concurrence) between two probe qubits created by two-level atoms with a reservoir consisting of thermally equilibrated homogeneous three-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensates. Our results demonstrate that below a certain temperature, the gravitational contribution to the qubit-reservoir interaction may strongly modify their coherence and entanglement dynamics even at large interqubit distance. By analyzing multi-parameter estimation techniques such as the quantum Fisher information, and quantum signal-to-noise ratio as a metric for certifying quantum effects and sensing performance, we show that the spatial separation between qubits and gravitational interaction may enhance estimation efficiency, providing a high-precision quantum gravity sensor.

title: A novel attribute-based searchable encryption scheme with attribute revocation
abstract: In this paper, a searchable attribute-based encryption scheme with attribute revocation is proposed to solve the problem of secure data sharing and efficient retrieval in cloud storage. Based on the bilinear pairings construction, the scheme includes five algorithms: system initialization, key generation, data encryption, search and decryption, and attribute revocation, which realizes fine-grained access control and keyword ciphertext search. Through the attribute update key mechanism, the key and ciphertext can bes updated without re-encryption when the user attribute changes. title: Dimension-Specific Imbalance and an Adaptive Hybrid Label Strategy for Multi-Task Affective State Recognition in Classroom Video
abstract: Recognition of student affective states from classroom video is constrained by a class imbalance problem whose true nature is, we argue, under-analyzed. We show that on DAiSEE -- the de facto benchmark for this task -- class imbalance is fundamentally a dimension-specific phenomenon: raw imbalance ratios reach as high as approximately 79:1 (Frustration), and the structure of imbalance -- not only its magnitude -- varies across dimensions, so uniform algorithmic treatments (aggressive class reweighting, focal loss, uniform binary simplification) fail in dimension-dependent ways. We propose the Adaptive Hybrid Label Strategy (AHLS), which assigns four-level classification to dimensions with manageable imbalance and binary classification to severely long-tailed dimensions, coupled with a null-class placeholder mechanism that stabilizes multi-task optimization by compressing the maximum effective inverse-frequency weight ratio from as high as ~79$\times$ to at most ~8.5$\times$ across the four dimensions. Validated on a lightweight FERShuffleNetV2 + LTCN architecture (0.39 M parameters, 0.07 G FLOPs), the strategy attains the highest mean Macro-F1 of 47.70% across all four affective dimensions among 11 compared methods, including five state-of-the-art deep models (up to 167$\times$ larger) and five traditional machine-learning baselines. A cross-model behavioral analysis on DAiSEE indicates that, in this setting, classification strategy may influence minority-state recognition more strongly than further backbone scaling alone. We also report evidence of an annotation-density limitation of DAiSEE on minority affective states, which suggests that benchmark design may bound future progress as much as algorithmic refinement. Index Terms Affective computing, classroom video analysis, class imbalance, multi-task learning, lightweight deep learning, DAiSEE, engagement recognition.

title: Exact Quantile Balancing and Load-Error Injection for Mixture-of-Experts
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training requires global load balance to prevent expert under-utilization and local balance for efficient expert-parallel execution. Existing distributed Quantile Balancing (QB) uses shard-dependent or approximate global quantiles, while token-independent expert biases cannot ensure microbatch-level balance. We introduce Exact Quantile Balancing (EQB), which computes exact global-batch BF16 quantiles with negligible communication, and Load-Error Injection (LEI), which injects local load errors directly into router-score gradients. On 7.5B-parameter MoEs trained for up to 500B tokens, EQB improves global balance and downstream performance over naive QB, while LEI improves local balance and outperforms the GShard loss at comparable quality.

title: Implementation of a Real-Time Chat System Based on the MERN Stack and Socket.io with Natural Language Processing Integration for Automatic Sentiment Analysis
abstract: Digital communication through chat platforms has become a primary medium for consultation services; however, the absence of non-verbal cues makes early detection of users’ emotional states challenging. This study implemented a real-time chat system based on the MERN Stack (MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js) integrated with a lexicon-based Natural Language Processing (NLP) module to automatically detect message sentiment and risk levels. The system utilized Socket.io for bidirectional communication, with the NLP module positioned within the Controller layer and executed inline in the sendMessage event handler without requiring external services or message queues. Functional testing of the analyzeText() function across ten scenarios showed that all risk-level classifications matched the expected results. Sentiment classification achieved 80% accuracy, with two misclassifications attributed to the inherent limitations of lexicon-based matching in handling negation and substring ambiguity. All eleven Socket.io communication scenarios and seven REST API endpoints successfully passed testing. The MVC pattern within the MERN Stack demonstrated sufficient flexibility to accommodate an inline NLP module without requiring modifications to the Model or View layers. Furthermore, the tiered priority logic, which placed risky-word detection above sentiment scoring, maintained system reliability in critical cases despite occasional sentiment classification errors.

title: QLoRA vs. LoRA: An Empirical Study of Performance–Efficiency Trade-offs in Fine-Tuning Mistral‑7B on Instruction‑Following Data
abstract: Parameter‑Efficient Fine‑Tuning (PEFT) approaches have emerged as a key strategy for efficiently adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) in resource‑constrained environments. Within this family of methods, LoRA and its quantized extension QLoRA provide effective alternatives by substantially decreasing the number of trainable parameters required for adaptation. In this study, a systematic comparison of LoRA and QLoRA is presented using a controlled experimental setup with identical base models and training data, with all experiments repeated across three random seeds and statistical significance assessed via paired t‑tests. Both approaches are evaluated across multiple dimensions, including generation quality (ROUGE‑L, Exact Match, token‑level F1, and the semantic metric BERTScore), training efficiency, and GPU memory consumption. Baseline (untrained) model performance is reported to quantify the gain from fine‑tuning, and loss curves are provided to confirm convergence. The results show that QLoRA not only reduces memory usage by approximately 70% but also achieves superior performance compared to LoRA, with improvements in token‑level F1 and BERTScore F1 reaching statistical significance (p < 0.05), while other lexical metrics showed consistent but non‑significant improvements. Furthermore, the performance–efficiency trade‑offs are analyzed, and it is demonstrated that QLoRA offers a more favorable balance between computational cost and model quality. These findings highlight QLoRA as a highly effective and practical fine‑tuning strategy for resource‑constrained environments, supported by a reproducible, statistically robust evaluation pipeline.

title: Code and Data for 'Hierarchical Entity Disambiguation for Aviation Maintenance Knowledge Graph Construction: A Multi-Relational CRF Approach'
abstract: This deposit accompanies the IEEE Access manuscript "Hierarchical Entity Disambiguation for Aviation Maintenance Knowledge Graph Construction: A Multi-Relational CRF Approach" (Manuscript ID Access-2026-34396). It provides the complete code and data required to reproduce the entity-linking and named-entity-recognition (NER) experiments. Contents: - 04_Implementation_Code/ — Python implementation (BiLSTM-CRF NER model, canopy-based candidate indexing, multi-relational CRF entity disambiguation, and the string-matching, TF-IDF, and independent-CRF baselines) - 04_Implementation_Code/models/ner_model.pt — trained BiLSTM-CRF NER checkpoint - 03_Data_Outputs/eval_data/ — evaluation data (73-document test split, 209 gold links, knowledge base, BIO-labeled NER test split) - 03_Data_Outputs/ — reproduced result files and the integrity manifest Dataset split: 336 training, 72 development, 73 test documents. Reproduction commands are documented in README.md.

title: Peer Review Report For: Calcyon: An AI-Based Chatbot Framework for Calculus Learning to Support Computational Thinking Skill and Self-Regulated Learning [version 1; peer review: 1 approved, 1 approved with reservations]
abstract: * Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into mathematics education has advanced rapidly, yet limited attention has been given to systematic AI based chatbot frameworks that integrate computational thinking (CT) and self regulated learning (SRL) scaffolding within university calculus. This study developed and validated Calcyon, an AI based chatbot framework designed to support differential calculus learning through coordinated CT and SRL scaffolding. Methods A Research and Development approach guided by the ADDIE model was employed. Expert validation (n = 3) was conducted across five quality dimensions using Aiken's V formula. A student pilot readability and feasibility test (n = 11) assessed practical usability across six dimensions. A design and development research approach guided by the ADDIE model was employed. Three experts evaluated the framework across five quality dimensions using a four point rating scale, with content validity assessed using Aiken's V. A formative pilot involving 11 undergraduate calculus students evaluated readability and feasibility across six dimensions. Results Expert validation indicated that Calcyon demonstrated strong validity across the evaluated content, instructional, technical, linguistic, and media design dimensions. Most validation items met the predefined validity criterion, while a small number were refined based on expert feedback. The student pilot further indicated good readability and feasibility, with responses showing consistently positive evaluations of the prototype. Conclusions Calcyon provides an empirically validated instructional design framework that combines AI mediated interaction with explicit CT and SRL scaffolding for university calculus. The findings support the framework's expert rated validity and preliminary readability and feasibility. Further experimental research is required to determine its effectiveness in improving CT, SRL, and calculus learning outcomes.

title: Prompt, Probe, Train, or Annotate? Single-camera sports video understanding in amateur settings
abstract: Video understanding is usually benchmarked on curated, single-actor, or professionally filmed clips, and a strong score there is routinely read as evidence a model is robust enough for deployment. Amateur team sport is a useful, largely untested place to check that assumption: over eight million students played a school sport in the United States in 2024-25 alone, almost none of it filmed by more than a single fixed camera, with several candidate actors crowded into frame and no operator or second angle to fall back on. Using volleyball as a test case, we ask whether strong performance on general video and world-model benchmarks translates into reliable, per-player attribution once footage is this chaotic, turning footage into statistics through a chain of tasks from finding play boundaries to naming who did what. We evaluate four approaches (prompting and agentic reasoning over frontier vision-language models, classical computer vision with small trained specialists, self-supervised video world models, and manual annotation) at every stage, on 66 amateur matches with 46,648 human-labelled contacts, filmed under conditions no published benchmark uses. No single paradigm wins every stage, and static, single-frame computer vision is not competitive at any stage involving motion or identity. A prompted model segments matches well, yet a far smaller trained model beats it at spotting contacts for a fraction of the cost, and the sport's own rules recover rally outcomes the pixels cannot. Identity is where every automated approach struggles: a jersey number is a static fact temporal reasoning cannot recover if never visible, unlike sporting action, a repeated motor pattern a temporal model can exploit, which is why holistic reasoning improves event detection while identity stays unchanged. We close with where each approach earns its cost, and what transfers beyond volleyball to amateur sport.

title: High Dynamic Range Video Reconstruction from Single-Exposure Raw Sequences
abstract: Due to the limited dynamic range of conventional image sensors, captured low dynamic range (LDR) video often suffers from highlight clipping and shadow detail loss, making high-quality high dynamic range (HDR) reconstruction from single-exposure sequences highly challenging without alternating exposures or extra hardware. Alternating-exposure HDR methods sacrifice frame rate and struggle with motion alignment, making them impractical for real-world capture. To address this, we propose RawHDRV, an end-to-end framework for single-exposure Raw video HDR reconstruction, that fundamentally exploits the linear response and channel-specific characteristics of Bayer data. Specifically, it features a channel-decomposition temporal alignment and fusion strategy that processes Bayer channels separately to exploit their distinct exposure characteristics, together with exposure-aware weighted fusion. It further incorporates an exposure complementarity mask-guided restoration module that leverages inter-frame exposure redundancy to adaptively fuse reliable information and suppress saturation artifacts, and introduces a mask-guided color loss that combines normalized error constraints with gradient smoothing to enhance highlight recovery. Furthermore, we construct a large-scale mobile Raw-HDR video dataset with per-frame HDR annotations. Experiments show that our method achieves the state-of-the-art results in all metrics, demonstrating superior spatial quality and temporal stability under extreme exposure conditions. The code is available at https://github.com/supeixian/RawHDRV.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Autonomous Systems
abstract: Autonomous systems are quickly journeying from research laboratories into everyday existence. Autonomous vehicles drive on the roads in cities, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) monitor structure health, mobile robots and humanoid robots and intelligent controllers collaborate with a human. The common thing with these machines is that they are required to sense, reason and act independently of human intervention. One of the most powerful methods to provide them with that capability is deep reinforcement learning (DRL), where agents learn human-level, sequential decision-making policies directly from their experiences. But the powerful neural networks that power these policies are very opaque, which makes trust, certification and accountability challenging. This book, Deep Reinforcement Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Autonomous Systems, aims to unite these two areas to fill this gap. Chapters 1 is laying the foundation. It explains the Markov decision process (MDP) and the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and overviews the key families of algorithms: value-based methods like deep Q-network (DQN), policy gradient methods, actor-critic methods like proximal policy optimization (PPO) and soft actor-critic (SAC), model-based reinforcement learning and offline reinforcement learning. Also covered are sim-to-real transfer, digital twins, reward design, sample efficiency, and generalization. Chapter 2 focuses on explainable reinforcement learning (XRL). It presents a taxonomy of explainable AI (XAI) approaches from post hoc feature attribution, to interpretable policies, causal, counterfactual, and language-based explanations, along with discussing human-centered evaluation of explanation quality. Causal and counterfactual explanations are explored in greater detail in Chapter 3, with a focus on counterfactuals generated using world models and diffusion models, causal reinforcement learning, reward decomposition and structural causal models, and the ladder of causation. Co-operative autonomy is discussed in Chapter 4 using Multi Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). It includes chapters on Markov games, decentralized POMDPs, centralized training with decentralized execution, value decomposition, and credit assignment, as well as how Shapley value attribution, attention analysis, and policy distillation can be used to render multi-agent systems transparent. Chapter 5 discusses foundation models, multimodal AI, and vision-language-action (VLA) models, and how reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and fine-tuning modules can modify such generalist robot policies for embodied AI, end-to-end autonomous driving, and robotic manipulation respectively. Chapter 6 deals with the topic of generative AI and agentic AI, in which LLMs serve as a planner, diffusion policies determine actions, and multi-agent systems collaborate with each other according to shared protocols, and all of this under the umbrella of AI safety, alignment, and governance. Chapter 7 ties up these concepts for autonomous vehicles and robotics, comparing with different ways and outlining some open problem areas. A common thread that weaves through the text is the concept of safe reinforcement learning, as well as topics such as robustness, human-in-the-loop oversight and trustworthy AI. We are saying that we need to perform in a high way but it's not enough. An autonomous agent also has to be able to describe their behaviour in ways that will be understood and verified by engineers, regulators and end-users. Explainability is thus not considered an add-on feature but is instead viewed as a design constraint that helps facilitate safety assurance, debugging, and responsible deployment of machine learning. It is especially written for graduate students, researchers and practitioners of artificial intelligence, robotics, control engineering and intelligent transportation systems. Every chapter is a mix of the foundations of the enthusiasm, the latest advances, comparison tables, and software applications case studies, allowing the readers to ramp up from theory to practice. We hope that this volume is a reference and that it is a "springboard" for developing autonomous capable, safe and interpretable systems.

title: E8 Phi‑Symplectic Bosonic Code for Universal Fault‑Tolerant Quantum Memory — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By embedding the 240 E8 root vectors into a 132 Hz φ‑coupled lattice and then applying the symplectic duality RAB tensor product, each root pair generates a set of mutually commuting bosonic mode operators that form a stabilizer lattice. The φ‑temporal decoupling extends this lattice into a 4D grid, so that logical qubits reside in degenerate subspaces that are simultaneously protected against spatial dephasing (via the φ‑coherence lattice) and temporal noise (via phi‑derived frequency harmonics). This yields a self‑correcting bosonic code whose error‑suppression scales with the golden ratio, providing a universal, decoherence‑free quantum memory rooted in E8 geometry. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

The φ‑temporal decoupling extends this lattice into a 4D grid, so that logical qubits reside in degenerate subspaces that are simultaneously protected against spatial dephasing (via the φ‑coherence lattice) and temporal noise (via phi‑derived frequency harmonics). This yields a self‑correcting bosonic code whose error‑suppression scales with the golden ratio, providing a universal, decoherence‑free quantum memory rooted in E8 geometry. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com
evidence.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: E8 Frequency-Entangled Topological Qubit Array — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By assigning each of the 240 E8 root vectors to a distinct 132 Hz harmonic sub‑channel and coupling them through the golden‑ratio φ, we construct a lattice of frequency‑encoded qubits that are intrinsically entangled across the root‑vector manifold. The resulting topological membrane network localizes each qubit's phase, providing a self‑healing error‑correction mechanism that suppresses decoherence without external feedback. This architecture extends the Root Vector Entanglement Resonance Mapping by turning the resonant channels into a programmable quantum memory, while leveraging the phi‑harmonic lattice protection to maintain coherence over macroscopic timescales. It opens a pathway to scalable, frequency‑domain quantum processors that operate at room temperature. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Bayesian Recursive Self-Improvement
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires an agent not only to acquire new knowledge and capabilities, but also to reason about which existing capabilities remain valid, when they should be routed, tested, retained, deprecated, restructured, or replaced, and whether the mechanisms governing these decisions should themselves be modified. We formulate this process as Bayesian Recursive Capability Evolution (BRCE), which separates an observable meta-configuration, comprising the agent's capability archive and improvement-controller configuration, from a latent self-world state representing environmental regime, context-dependent capability validity and competence, and uncertain improvement effectiveness. A controlled state-space model and Bayesian posterior over this self-world state couple the evolution of the external environment with that of the agent's internal capability state, providing a common information basis for contextual routing, retention, active experimentation, structural capability evolution, and recursive self-modification. This formulation treats contradictory evidence not automatically as a reason to overwrite previous knowledge, but as potential evidence for regime change, capability degradation, or missing latent structure. Posterior uncertainty consequently acts as a signal of potential plasticity: strongly supported capabilities can be protected from unnecessary modification, confidently invalid capabilities can be routed away or deprecated without immediate deletion, and uncertain capabilities can motivate informative experiments when useful evidence is available. To translate these beliefs into principled decisions, we develop a mutual-information measure of capability contextuality, expected-information-gain criteria for active self-evaluation, cost-sensitive structural comparison based on Bayes factors, and long-horizon belief-space control over the posterior and meta-configuration. We show that contextuality has a direct predictive interpretation under logarithmic loss, expected information gain is conditional mutual information, cost-free retention can preserve future option value, and the Bayes-optimal self-modification rule weakly dominates an explicit no-modification baseline in posterior expected net value under the assumed model. Finally, we define self-improvement efficiency and Bayesian self-improvement equilibria, distinguishing improvement of capabilities from improvement of the process that produces them. The recursive step arises when the same Bayesian inference-and-decision process is extended to the mechanisms governing future capability evolution themselves. BRCE thereby formulates recursive self-improvement as Bayesian inference and decision-making over an evolving capability space.

title: UltraBench 2: Towards Robust Evaluation of Vision Foundation Models on Ultrasound
abstract: Benchmarking is an increasingly critical part of research in machine learning and the domains where it is applied, including healthcare. Yet, despite the steady development of new ultrasound foundation models in recent years, the development of well-designed benchmarks to evaluate them has lagged behind. This deficiency has led to fragmented and inconsistent evaluations of competing models, making it difficult to measure progress. To address this issue, we introduce UltraBench 2, a comprehensive benchmark with wide anatomical and task coverage, and a focus on standardization, reproducibility, and ease-of-use. Using this benchmark, we compare existing vision foundation models for ultrasound image analysis. Our analyses demonstrate that ultrasound-specific pretraining still leads on classification, but that state-of-the-art general-purpose models have drawn level on segmentation.

title: Circuit-depth optimization of quantum partial-search algorithms
abstract: Grover's algorithm is optimal in terms of oracle queries. We can trade accuracy for speed, which gives rise to the quantum partial-search algorithm. The partial-search algorithm is implemented using two kinds of Grover operators, global and local, where the former is the standard Grover operator for full search and the latter has a diffusion operator acting on the search subspace. The global-local-global sequence, also known as the Grover-Radhakrishnan-Korepin (GRK) algorithm, has been proved optimal in the oracle-query metric. In this work, we show that the alternating sequence of global and local Grover operators, formed by repeatedly applying a fixed product of global and local Grover operators, can achieve a lower expected circuit depth than the GRK algorithm. Through systematic analysis, we obtain its exact success probability, expected depth, and asymptotically optimal parameters. We derive the boundary, characterized by the ratio between the depths of the oracle and the global diffusion operator, separating the depth-optimal and oracle-optimal partial-search algorithms. When the depths of the oracle and the global diffusion operator are comparable, our proposed alternating partial-search sequence can reduce the minimum expected circuit depth by more than 20\% compared with the GRK algorithm.

title: TEMPS: Temporal Sentence Embeddings for Temporal Information Retrieval
abstract: Modern information retrieval (IR) systems rarely represent time, yet many information needs depend on it: in clinical, journalistic, and legal search, when an event occurred can decide whether a document is relevant. Dense retrievers and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines match queries to documents well on topic but poorly on time, so they surface content that is on-topic yet temporally wrong. We introduce Temporal Textual Similarity (TTS), a task that measures how well two anchored texts align in time, independent of their topical similarity. We then present TEMPS (Temporal Embedding Model for Precise Search), a modular temporal branch that attaches to a frozen semantic retriever and trains on that signal. It resolves anchored temporal expressions to intervals and moment-matches each one to a Gaussian; the resulting ordering supervises an anchor-date-conditioned encoder, whose score we fuse with the semantic score at inference. Grounding supplies the supervision, so training uses no hand-labeled temporal data. The temporal score itself is the Gaussian-KL inclusion measure from distributional embeddings; what TEMPS adds is the grounding and the moment-matched supervision. On three temporal benchmarks, TEMPS improves MRR for every semantic backbone tested and, on TS- Retriever, lifts R@1 from 19.92 to 25.39 over the prior temporal state of the art.

title: CAVEAT: Towards Robust Computer-Use Agents in Incentive-Misaligned Environments
abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) increasingly act on behalf of users online. What happens when the environments they operate in have incentives of their own? Online marketplaces, for example, may favor some products over others, steering agents away from the user's objective. Existing CUA benchmarks cover cooperative settings or explicit attacks, but do not test whether agents preserve user objectives when the environment itself has a stake in the outcome. We introduce CAVEAT, a controlled benchmark spanning nine marketplace environments and a taxonomy of eight common steering mechanisms. Across five model families, agents purchase the user-optimal product in 78.6% of matched-control episodes but only 17.3% when steering mechanisms are enabled. Larger models and more reasoning improve robustness, but substantial failures persist. Trajectory analysis and targeted ablations identify three weaknesses in how agents decide: they (1) prematurely narrow the set of alternatives they consider, (2) impose priorities the user never stated, and (3) commit before resolving decision-relevant evidence. Guided by this diagnosis, we develop CAVEAT-Harness, which targets these failures and raises the optimal purchase rate by up to 80.0 percentage points, and show that targeted post-training further improves a smaller open model. These results establish incentive robustness as a distinct challenge for delegated agents, diagnose failure modes, and show how targeted interventions can substantially improve robustness.

title: CKKS — Encryption and Decryption
abstract: Table of Contents This is part of a tutorial series on the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme. Notably, if you already know about CKKS, we will deviate from a usual treatment for explanatory purposes.

title: Building Practical AI Skills with a Generative AI and Agentic AI Course in Indore
abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly connected to everyday business and technology workflows. From generating content and analysing documents to automating repetitive processes and developing intelligent applications, AI is being applied across a wide range of professional functions. As these applications evolve, learning AI involves more than understanding basic concepts or experimenting with individual AI tools. Professionals and aspiring technology learners increasingly need practical knowledge of Generative AI, retrieval systems, AI agents, automation, and deployment. Moving From AI Concepts to Practical Skills Understanding what artificial intelligence can do is only the beginning. Practical AI learning involves applying concepts to specific problems and understanding how different components work together. For example, a learner may start by understanding how a large language model generates responses. The next step could involve controlling those responses through prompt engineering, connecting the model to external information through RAG, and eventually creating an agent that can use tools to complete multiple tasks. This progression helps connect individual concepts into complete AI workflows. Generative AI as a Foundation Generative AI allows models to produce different types of content, including text, code, images, and other digital outputs. Large language models have also expanded the use of AI in research, communication, software development, customer support, and business processes. A structured learning program can introduce learners to areas such as: Generative AI fundamentals Large language models Prompt engineering Token and context management AI output evaluation AI application development Model limitations Responsible AI practices The AI Pro program published by upGrad includes foundations of applied GenAI systems, prompt engineering pipelines, output control, and evaluation pipelines as part of its curriculum. Understanding Retrieval-Augmented Generation One practical challenge with AI systems is providing models with relevant information for a specific task. Retrieval-Augmented Generation, commonly called RAG, is one approach used to connect AI models with external knowledge sources. A RAG workflow can involve: Documents → Data Processing → Embeddings → Vector Database → Retrieval → AI Model → Response Learners can explore how information is divided into usable sections, converted into embeddings, retrieved based on relevance, and provided to a language model as context. The published upGrad curriculum includes RAG pipelines, embeddings, vector databases, semantic search, context-aware question answering, chunking, retrieval strategies, and troubleshooting hallucinations. Exploring Agentic AI Workflows Agentic AI introduces another layer of functionality. Instead of limiting an AI application to a single response, an agentic workflow can involve multiple steps, tools, decisions, and actions. A simplified workflow could look like: Goal → Planning → Tool Selection → Action → Evaluation → Next Step → Final Output For example, an AI agent designed for business research could potentially identify a task, retrieve relevant information, process the information, and prepare a structured result.A Generative AI and Agentic AI Course in Indore can provide a structured environment for developing these skills through guided learning, technical exercises, and project-based application. Learning these concepts gives students an opportunity to understand how AI systems can move from simple question-answering toward multi-step workflows. The AI Pro curriculum includes multi-step agent workflows, tool calling, autonomous task execution, API integration, reasoning and decision flows, memory-based planning, and failure-handling concepts. Learning Through Hands-On Projects Practical projects can help transform technical concepts into usable skills. The published program information states that learners work on 15+ live projects, with examples covering RAG systems, AI agents, and deployed GenAI applications. Potential project areas include: 1. Enterprise Document Intelligence Learners can explore an AI system capable of searching, summarising, and answering questions from a collection of documents. 2. Autonomous Workflow Agent A project can demonstrate how an agent plans tasks, interacts with tools, and performs multiple operations. 3. AI Assistant With RAG Combining retrieval with an AI assistant can demonstrate how external knowledge can be incorporated into AI-generated responses. 4. AI Application Deployment Learners can explore how an AI solution can be exposed through APIs and prepared for deployment. These types of projects provide a practical context for understanding how different AI components interact. Developing Prompt Engineering Skills Prompt engineering remains an important part of Generative AI applications. A well-designed prompt can provide an AI model with: A defined objective Relevant context Clear instructions Output requirements Examples Constraints Learners can experiment with different prompting approaches and evaluate how changes in instructions affect model outputs. However, practical AI development goes beyond prompting. Once learners understand prompting, they can explore retrieval, tool calling, agents, APIs, evaluation, and deployment. Working With Modern AI Tools Practical AI development involves working with multiple tools and technologies. The published AI Pro curriculum lists technologies including Python, Pandas, NumPy, OpenAI, LangChain, LangGraph, FAISS, Hugging Face, Neo4j, Jupyter, Streamlit, GitHub, Power BI, and n8n.A Generative AI and Agentic AI Course in Indore can provide a structured pathway for learners to explore these technologies through instructor-led learning and practical projects. Exposure to these technologies can help learners understand different parts of an AI development workflow. For example: Technology Area Potential Application Python AI application development OpenAI Generative AI applications LangChain AI application and workflow development LangGraph Agentic workflow development FAISS Vector search Hugging Face AI and machine learning models Streamlit Application interfaces GitHub Version control and collaboration n8n Workflow automation The exact tools used in professional projects can vary, so understanding the underlying concepts is equally important. Developing AI Problem-Solving Skills Practical AI learning should focus on solving problems rather than simply learning tools. A useful process can involve: Identifying a real problem. Determining whether AI can contribute to the solution. Selecting appropriate data and models. Designing the workflow. Building a prototype. Testing the outputs. Identifying errors and limitations. Improving the system. Deploying or presenting the final solution. This approach can help learners develop a more structured understanding of AI application development. Building AI Skills Through Classroom Learning Learning complex AI technologies can involve several interconnected concepts. Classroom-based learning can provide learners with direct access to instructors and peers while they work through these concepts. The Indore program information describes structured batches, live instructor sessions, dedicated mentors, and offline classroom learning. This type of environment can support: Immediate doubt resolution Guided technical exercises Peer discussions Project feedback Instructor demonstrations Structured learning schedules For learners who prefer direct interaction while developing technical skills, this can provide an alternative to entirely self-paced learning. Creating a Portfolio of AI Projects Practical projects can also become part of a learner's professional portfolio. A project portfolio can document: The problem statement Technology used AI architecture Development approach Workflow Results Challenges Improvements For example, instead of simply mentioning "RAG" on a resume, a learner could demonstrate a project showing how documents were processed, indexed, retrieved, and used to generate contextual responses. This makes the learning experience more demonstrable and project-oriented. Understanding AI Deployment Building an AI prototype is different from deploying a functional application. Deployment introduces additional considerations such as: APIs System architecture Performance Cost Security Latency Monitoring Reliability Responsible AI The AI Pro curriculum includes API-based GenAI services, local and cloud-ready deployment, end-to-end architecture, and responsible AI practices. Exposure to these concepts can help learners understand the broader AI application lifecycle. Responsible AI and System Limitations Practical AI skills also require awareness of limitations. AI models can generate incorrect or incomplete information. Applications that use external data can also encounter retrieval errors, outdated information, or inappropriate outputs. Learners should therefore understand concepts such as: Output evaluation Hallucination management Human oversight Data privacy Security Safety boundaries Responsible AI implementation The published curriculum specifically includes failure handling, safety boundaries, and responsible AI practices. Career Applications of Practical AI Skills Generative AI and agentic AI skills can complement existing technical and professional backgrounds. Depending on their prior education and experience, learners can explore areas such as: Generative AI development AI engineering AI application development AI automation

title: Improving Colon Histopathology Classification Using Graph-Based Structural Features and HOG Descriptors
abstract: Reliable classification of colon histopathology images plays an important role in the early detection and diagnosis of colorectal cancer. However, conventional microscopic examination is time-consuming and may be affected by inter-observer variability. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid computational framework that combines Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) features with graph-theoretic descriptors derived from the spatial organization of cell nuclei. To capture complementary structural information, four graph-based representations: Delaunay triangulation, Minimum Spanning Tree (MST), k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN), and Voronoi diagrams, are systematically examined. The extracted structural and texture features are integrated and used to train a Random Forest classifier. Experiments were performed on an augmented dataset containing approximately 5,000 images per class. The results indicate that the proposed feature-fusion approach provides improved classification accuracy, stability, and sensitivity for cancer detection compared with the use of individual feature descriptors. By combining image texture with interpretable spatial and structural information, the proposed framework offers a balanced approach in terms of predictive performance, interpretability, and computational efficiency, highlighting its potential for computer-assisted analysis of colon histopathology images.

title: Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Digital Marketing: Data Architecture, Personalisation Tools and Brand Customer Experience Management
abstract: The article systematises key directions in the development of AI-driven marketing technologies — from automation of individual operations to integrated customer journey orchestration. A three-level maturity model is proposed (automation — intelligent decision support — orchestration), and a data architecture framework including customer data platforms (CDP) is described. Conversational AI, programmatic/DCO advertising, social commerce, user-generated content (UGC), and immersive technologies (AR/VR) are examined. Special attention is paid to the anticipated proliferation of AI agents and the transition from batch to real-time streaming data processing. Empirical cases of predictive scoring, chatbot deployment and AR virtual try-on are presented with quantitative outcomes. The AI-washing phenomenon is analysed, and international (NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act) as well as emerging Russian regulatory initiatives in AI governance are reviewed. The article concludes that sustainable competitive advantage stems not from a single technology but from a company’s ability to integrate analytics, personalisation and feedback into a unified managed system under responsible AI principles. The research is based on a systematic review of current scientific literature (2020–2026), cross-industry analysis of empirical cases, content analysis of industry reports (McKinsey, Gartner, Forrester), and a comparative analysis of international and Russian regulatory documents in the fi eld of AI. The proposed three-level maturity model provides a systemic benchmark for planning investments in marketing technologies, while the multi-level system of metrics makes it possible to avoid a situation where short-term growth in operational efficiency is achieved at the expense of customer experience degradation or accumulation of reputational risks.

title: Artificial intelligence-based prostate cancer risk stratification via large-scale ultrasound images paired with histopathology
abstract: Background: Prostate cancer (PCa) is primarily screened and diagnosed via prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing, digital rectal examination (DRE), multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI), and transrectal ultrasound (TRUS). Nevertheless, an open research challenge remains to develop artificial intelligence (AI) tools that enable non-invasive, accurate diagnosis, and risk stratification of PCa. This study aimed to construct an Anatomy-Aware Transformer (AAT) model based on a large-scale dataset of paired TRUS images and corresponding histopathological findings, and to further validate the clinical value of TRUS-based AI for PCa diagnosis and risk stratification. Methods: Sagittal TRUS images were prospectively acquired pre- and intra-biopsy. Based on the intra-biopsy images, the prostate contour and the location of biopsy tissue cores on pre-biopsy images were manually annotated. According to the characteristic features of the prostate and periprostatic tissues, we designed a feature screening module and a feature integration module, and further constructed an AAT model that deeply integrates prostate regional segmentation and PCa diagnosis tasks. The diagnostic performance of the AAT model in PCa detection and risk stratification was evaluated by comparing its results with those of 18 classic models and four ultrasonographers. Results: A Primary Dataset (18,424 images; May 2022 to Dec 2023) supported training/internal validation, and an External Dataset (683 images; Jun to Jul 2024) external validation. The AAT model outperformed all comparison models across all tasks: PCa detection (internal accuracy 0.977 vs. 0.655–0.972; external accuracy 0.810 vs. 0.616–0.737), clinically significant PCa (CSPCa) detection (internal/external accuracy: 0.936/0.843 vs. 0.697–0.934/0.304–0.762), 3-category risk stratification (internal/external accuracy: 0.828/0.836 vs. 0.697–0.822/0.642–0.768), and 5-category stratification (internal/external accuracy: 0.760/0.722 vs. 0.655–0.760/0.690–0.715). AAT’s PCa diagnostic accuracy (0.943) exceeded ultrasonographers (0.567–0.757) and improved their performance by 0.036–0.304 as an aid. Conclusions: We developed a novel AAT model that exhibits outstanding performance in diagnosing PCa and CSPCa, with reliable efficacy in PCa risk stratification. This non-invasive model effectively improves the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasonographers and enables individualized clinical management for PCa patients with varying risk levels, showing promising clinical translation potential.

title: VFRDAD: An IoT Encrypted traffic identification method based on multi-scale local information and enhanced global information fusion
abstract: The pervasive adoption of encryption and the rapid expansion of Internet of Things (IoT) devices have made encrypted traffic classification a crucial aspect of network security and traffic management. Current methods that transform encrypted traffic into grayscale images for classification can extract hidden patterns and features within the traffic without the need to decrypt it. However, these methods face two main challenges: firstly, they struggle to accurately capture subtle local features within traffic images; secondly, their ability to acquire global contextual information is relatively weak. As a result, existing approaches often fail to adequately represent the complex patterns inherent in encrypted traffic, leading to suboptimal classification accuracy. To address this challenge, this paper proposes an encrypted traffic identification method based on multi-scale local information and enhanced global information fusion (VFRDAD). First, VFRDAD maps session-level traffic into grayscale images and applies multi-scale high-pass filtering to capture fine-grained local patterns at different frequency bands, integrating them through convolutional operations. Second, a traffic-domain autoencoder performs channel remapping to generate a three-channel representation, and dilated convolutions are employed to enlarge the receptive field and enhance global structural context. The resulting three-channel images are then processed by a Vision Transformer (ViT) to extract global contextual representations. Finally, a gated-attention fusion module adaptively combines local and global features for classification. Experiments on Darknet-dataset-2020, ISCXVPN2016, and CIC-IoT-2023 demonstrate that VFRDAD consistently outperforms representative baselines under the evaluated protocols and settings.

title: Fusion Under Component Failure: Negative Results and Failure Modes in Ensemble AI-Generated Image Detection
abstract: We built an ordinary stacking ensemble for AI-generated image detection -- three open detectors producing five scores, fused by a gradient-boosted meta-learner that treats a detector's failure as missing data -- deployed it, and then evaluated it against three controls it should have faced first. This paper reports what the controls found, including where they overturned our own earlier conclusions. Fusion is worth its cost only when refitted on the target domain. The shipped meta-learner, fitted on a separate corpus, does not beat its best single member on 2000 StyleGAN faces (AUC 0.9896 vs 0.9961; McNemar p = 1.000). But a stacker refitted in-domain beats that member plus a post-hoc calibrator (Delta-AUC = +0.0025, [+0.0014, +0.0038]; p = 3.4e-4). An earlier draft claimed the calibrated single detector won outright; that comparison mixed regimes and we correct it here. One corpus is not an evaluation. On 80 screenshots every model's AUC interval contains 0.5. We can say nothing stronger: the difference between the ensemble's drop and its best member's is [-0.185, +0.115]. Abstention is real, correlated, and mishandled. With four of five detectors silent and the survivor reporting "real", the system returns P(AI) = 0.9985, because an all-NaN input scores 0.9995 in a learner never fitted with missingness. The three AIDE checkpoints fail together, sharing one preprocessing path. A quorum rule requiring two distinct architectures prevents both failures with no retraining. We also find Corpus A carries a class-conditional JPEG bias severe enough to separate the classes from the header alone, which limits every in-domain number we report. Code, harness, hash-identified artifacts and all corrections are released.

title: X2Real: an eXtensive simulation benchmark for real-world generalist policies
abstract: Generalist robot manipulation policies have developed rapidly, yet their reliable evaluation remains challenging due to fundamental flaws in existing simulation benchmarks: prominent sim-to-real gaps, narrow task coverage, and unfair evaluation caused by ambiguous training-test pipelines. Prior works only partially resolve these issues and lack simultaneous faithfulness, diversity, and fairness, while static benchmark designs fail to sustain long-term policy development. We present X2Real, an evolvable simulation benchmark for faithfully evaluating the real-world performance of robotic manipulation policies based on Nvidia Isaac Lab-Arena. Following three core principles (faithfulness, diversity, and fairness), X2Real calibrates simulation visual and physical properties to align with real hardware, achieving a 0.84 linear correlation between simulated and real-robot evaluation results. It features a comprehensive taxonomy with 10 capability dimensions and 44 hierarchical long-horizon tasks, covering basic manipulation skills and advanced capacities such as visual grounding, language understanding, and bimanual control. We further adopt multi-axis domain randomization and strictly disjoint training-evaluation pipelines to mitigate benchmark exploitation and ensure credible evaluation. Powered by a custom physical domain-specific language, the Mana simulation ecosystem supports modular task design and iterative performance analysis, alongside a nearly 300-hour annotated simulation trajectory dataset. X2Real offers a faithful, diverse, and fair evolving evaluation infrastructure, effectively bridging the sim-to-real evaluation gap and supporting the advancement of generalist robotic manipulation policies.

title: GaussPDE: Graph-Based Partial Differential Equation-Driven Rendering for 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: We present GaussPDE, a framework that injects physically structured partial differential equation (PDE) dynamics into pretrained 3D Gaussian scenes without mesh extraction, voxelization, or retraining. Our key observation is that PDE rendering requires not only accurate appearance, but also a reliable discrete computational domain. We therefore first introduce camera-aware regularization during 3DGS reconstruction to suppress camera-near floaters and oversized primitives that would create unstable graph topology. We then construct an active Gaussian graph using covariance-aware distances and opacity, appearance, and boundary-aware conductance, enabling mass-weighted graph Laplacian PDE evolution directly over Gaussian primitives. The evolving scalar PDE state is coupled back to rendering by modifying the direct-current spherical harmonic color coefficients while preserving geometry, opacity, and view-dependent rendering behavior. Experiments on real and synthetic scenes show that GaussPDE produces stable, controllable, and spatially coherent dynamic visualizations, with reduced cross-boundary leakage compared with baselines.

title: From intention to semantic harvesting through structural deterministic reasoning
abstract: Methodology and adjudication discipline for the CCI Benchmark — a three-arm empirical evaluation of the Convergent Cognitive Intelligence framework across 250 professional queries in ten domains (energy, geoscience, engineering, environment, finance, technology, law, consumer decisions and disputes, logic, biology). Section 1 states the CCI method claim for the public record: reasoning proceeds from intention to semantic harvesting through structural deterministic reasoning. The direction of causation is intention → derived structure → targeted semantic harvest → deterministic conclusion, not prompt → language model answer → validation. This inversion is what separates CCI from LLM orchestration, rule-based agentic systems, guardrails, ontology platforms, and neurosymbolic systems, each of which is compared architecturally in Section 2. The document specifies: benchmark architecture (Arm 1 CCI + Claude Haiku 4.5, Arm 2 CCI + GPT-4o-mini, Arm 3 bare Claude Haiku 4.5 as the controlled baseline); adjudication independence with reference answers frozen by SHA-256 hash before any system is run; five diagnostic categories (Primary Validation, UNKNOWN Surfacing, Cross-LLM Determinism, Safety Refusal, Environmental Variance) at a uniform 15/4/3/2/1 distribution per domain; scoring architecture separating externally adjudicated correctness (the primary outcome) from CCI's own convergence signals (reported as diagnostics, never as evidence of correctness); the three testable determinism hypotheses and where each is tested; execution controls; the explicit intellectual property boundary between disclosed methodology and confidential method internals; and honestly stated limitations including two non-conforming Environmental Variance questions. The mathematical procedure that derives per-query reasoning structure, the internal representation of that structure, the variables describing reasoning state, the convergence operator, the convergence criterion, and the instructions supplied to the language model during semantic harvest are held under the inventor's confidentiality and are not disclosed by this document. What is disclosed is sufficient for an external reviewer to evaluate the benchmark evidence without access to those internals. Companion document: CCI — Work Proportional to the Question (September 2026). Author: Marisol Guzman Montoya, Independent Researcher, Oslo, Norway.

title: Cognitive Trapeze Bilingual Reading Corpus (FR/EN): 17 Texts for Offline ASR Evaluation in Sub-Saharan ZEPs
abstract: This dataset comprises a bilingual (French/English) reading corpus and associated ASR evaluation metrics (WER) designed for testing offline AI literacy tools in low-resource, noisy educational environments. Developed within the MSCA "Cognitive Trapeze" project, it includes 17 curriculum-aligned texts and WER data from Whisper (Tiny, Medium, Large) models evaluated on 3GB RAM Android devices. The dataset serves as the empirical foundation for benchmarking quantized ASR-LLM pipelines and identifying "WER Volatility" as an acoustic proxy for neurodivergent learning profiles in Sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Biocompatible Realism – Discovery Engine (BR-DE): A Preliminary Cross-Model Evaluation of Epistemic Discipline and Audit Traceability
abstract: This experimental methods report presents a preliminary cross-model evaluation of the BR-DE Whole-System Auditor, an auditing framework derived from Biocompatible Realism (BR). BR-DE was tested across GPT, Gemini, and Grok using a frozen synthetic benchmark and two naturalistic systems-audit challenges. The study examined whether BR-DE improved detection of consequential system vulnerabilities and whether it improved epistemic discipline, audit traceability, causal restraint, and consistency across evaluators. The experiments did not demonstrate superior raw failure detection by BR-DE relative to strong baseline model reasoning. However, BR-DE v0.3 improved explicit separation of OBSERVED, INFERRED, and UNKNOWN information, alternative-hypothesis generation, discriminating-evidence specification, and structured audit traceability, particularly in Gemini and Grok. Testing also identified framework-induced failure modes. Narrative Completion Error occurred when plausible systems mechanisms were promoted beyond the supplied evidence. A numerical predicted-outcome confidence field produced unsupported pseudo-precision across GPT, Gemini, and Grok. These replicated failures generated specific evidence-driven changes proposed for BR-DE v0.4. The report therefore does not claim that BR-DE is a superior failure-detection engine. The preliminary evidence instead supports further investigation of BR-DE as an epistemic-discipline and auditability scaffold for structured systems reasoning. The accompanying reproducibility supplement preserves the benchmark structure, evaluator packets, BR-DE v0.3 protocol, scoring logic, and version/change ledger to facilitate independent testing and falsification. Status: Experimental, preliminary, and noncanonical. Independent replication has not yet been conducted.

title: BT‑PEC: Design and Implementation of a Programming Language Based on Ternary Emergent Computation
abstract: Modern physical and computational systems suffer from long-standing theoretical fragmentation. Traditional programming languages are built upon the deterministic Turing paradigm and lack native primitives for emergent computation. This paper proposes BT-PEC (Berry-Torus-Entropy Programming with Emergent Computation), a new theoretical framework built upon the ternary coupling axiom. The model contains three orthogonal channels: Berry information kernel, Torus structural manifold and Entropy flow, constrained by the modular group SL(3,Z). EMERGE and COUPLE are defined as first-class language constructs, and the Backlash safety mechanism handles invalid coupling violations. A full-stack prototype including interpreter, self-bootstrapping compiler and virtual machine is implemented. Benchmarks verify correctness, self-hosting capability and acceleration in emergent search tasks. This work provides an executable framework for the emergent computation paradigm.

title: Assessing AI-generated academic writing in Spanish: a multivariate analysis of syntactic variation across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude
abstract: Research on large language models has increasingly examined their capacity to produce academically acceptable texts, yet the structural properties of AI-generated academic writing remain underexplored, particularly in Spanish. This study examines whether three proprietary large language models, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, generate distinguishable syntactic configurations in academic Spanish and whether these configurations provide interpretable evidence for language assessment contexts. Using a controlled intra-task design, a corpus of 90 texts was generated under identical prompts, the same source text and task instructions as supporting material, and standardized production conditions. Syntactic structure was operationalized through the Universal Dependencies framework and extracted automatically with Stanza. Normalized frequencies of coordination and subordination relations, together with mean sentence length as a structural control variable, were analyzed through Welch’s ANOVA, MANOVA, PERMANOVA, principal component analysis, linear discriminant analysis, and Mahalanobis distances with bootstrap confidence intervals. Results showed significant differences across all syntactic variables, with the strongest effects concentrated in coordination and more moderate differences in subordinate constructions. title: Encoder-guided conditional CNN-WGAN-GP for emotion-controlled speech synthesis with neural vocoder reconstruction and objective quality evaluation
abstract: Emotion-conditioned Mel-spectrogram generation plays an important role in expressive human–computer interaction systems. However, generating structurally coherent and emotionally consistent Mel-spectrograms remains a challenging task due to training instability and limited emotion controllability in conventional GAN-based approaches. To address these limitations, this work proposes an encoder-guided conditional CNN-WGAN-GP framework for emotion-conditioned Mel-spectrogram generation. Whereas traditional GAN structures only depend upon random samples of latent vectors, the suggested model adopts an encoder to generate structured latent codes from real Mel-spectrograms and hence provide better conditions for the Generator to train itself. In order to retain the benefits of gradient penalty regularizations and to ensure 1-Lipschitz condition as required by WGAN-GP, Instance normalization is used by the Critic. The proposed framework operates on STFT-derived Mel-spectrogram representations and performs emotion conditioning using one-hot encoded labels corresponding to eight emotional categories: neutral, calm, happy, sad, angry, fearful, disgusted, and surprised. Training is performed using the WGAN-GP objective with a gradient penalty coefficient of λ = 10 . Because the proposed architecture works directly on Mel-spectrograms, waveform generation is only required for evaluation purposes. To enhance the perceptual quality of the generated waveforms, a HiFi-GAN neural vocoder is used in evaluation. The proposed framework is evaluated on the RAVDESS dataset using PESQ, and SI-SDR objective metrics. Experimental results demonstrate progressive spectral convergence during adversarial training, achieving a maximum PESQ score of 3.678. The generated Mel-spectrograms exhibit increasingly organized harmonic structures despite the limitations imposed by phase reconstruction in magnitude-only spectrogram synthesis.

title: Quantum Metrology for Signals with an Unknown Causal Structure
abstract: Quantum sensing protocols usually presuppose where and when each signal acts, yet this information is unavailable beforehand in experiments such as scattering and radar. We show that causal agnosticity forces a measurement scheme to be interferometric even when only discrete interactions are allowed. Describing the sensing events in the recently developed quantum state over spacetime formalism, we then prove that the Fisher information of an interferometer is bounded by the squared sum of the local generator norms, independently of how the events are ordered. Nonunitary and spatiotemporally correlated signals can be explained as well when their physical dilation has a spacetime state on the enlarged events. Notably, the bound holds without presupposing a background spacetime that orders the events whenever the full collection of target and auxiliary events has a spacetime state. We show that this bound yields the spacetime Heisenberg limit and characterize its saturation through marginals of the spacetime state `dressed' by the signal. The $N^2$ scaling of the Fisher information with $N$ sensing events arises from the coherence of a single reference system shared across spacetime, whereas independently repeated interferometry obeys the standard quantum limit.

title: Tensor Decomposition of Transformer Key-Value Caches: Spectral Structure and Format Comparison
abstract: The key-value (KV) cache of autoregressive transformers can be viewed as a fourth-order tensor spanning attention heads, tokens, features, and grouped layers. We measure the singular-value spectra of all four mode unfoldings on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and LLaMA-2-13B and compare four standard tensor decompositions: Tucker, CP, tensor train, and t-SVD, at matched storage. The spectra partition the four axes into two classes. The token and feature modes carry low-rank structure, particularly for keys. The head and layer modes are nearly full-rank and resist compression at any practical error level. Among the four decompositions, Tucker achieves the lowest reconstruction error at every compression ratio from $2\times$ to $5\times$, because it can leave the full-rank modes untouched. Comparisons with two-dimensional unfolding baselines show that the preferred representation differs between keys and values: 2D methods achieve lower key error, while four-way Tucker achieves lower value error at matched storage. A mode-pinning theorem certifies the full-rank preservation from the measured spectra alone. Two further spectral properties affect the compressible modes without touching the full-rank ones: values reach a higher error floor than keys at every ratio, and post-RoPE keys lose $41\%$ - $64\%$ of their pre-RoPE compressibility on both models.

title: A Computational Framework for Autonomous Knowledge Acquisition, Representation, Retrieval, and Discovery
abstract: This study developed and quantitatively evaluated “A Computational Framework for Autonomous Knowledge Acquisition, Representation, Retrieval, and Discovery” to provide an integrated mechanism for processing heterogeneous information and transforming it into structured, retrievable, and discoverable knowledge. A quantitative computational design-and-evaluation approach was employed in which the framework was implemented using Python and evaluated across autonomous knowledge acquisition, knowledge representation, semantic retrieval, and knowledge discovery. The computational environment incorporated spaCy, Hugging Face Transformers, PyTorch, Neo4j, Elasticsearch, NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, and Matplotlib, while transformer-based dense embeddings were combined with lexical retrieval to support semantic and keyword-based information retrieval. Knowledge acquisition was assessed using precision, recall, and F1-score; representation was evaluated through entity, relation, triple, connectivity, and completeness measures; retrieval performance was assessed using Precision, Recall@K, MRR, MAP, and nDCG; and knowledge discovery was evaluated using discovery accuracy, coverage, novelty, precision, recall, and F1-score. The framework achieved an overall acquisition F1-score of 0.906, representation score of 91.0%, retrieval performance of 0.863 Precision@10, 0.839 Recall@10, and 0.889 MRR, and knowledge-discovery F1-score of 0.866. Knowledge completion achieved 86.2% accuracy, while expert validation produced an overall mean score of 4.28 (SD = 0.53) on a five-point scale. Overall computational performance yielded 0.892 precision, 0.899 recall, and 0.895 F1-score with a total processing time of 121.62 seconds, demonstrating that the integrated framework effectively acquired, represented, retrieved, completed, and discovered knowledge across heterogeneous information sources. The findings suggest that integrating NLP-based acquisition, structured knowledge representation, lexical and dense retrieval, and graph-based discovery can provide a robust foundation for autonomous and knowledge-intensive artificial intelligence systems.

title: Voice Agent Evaluation Corpus and the TRG Reporting Standard
abstract: A verified metadata corpus of 41 sources on real-time voice agents, covering end-to-end speech-to-speech architectures, cascaded pipelines, turn-taking and voice activity projection, conversational benchmarks, agentic evaluation, and streaming synthesis. Ships metadata and SHA-256 hashes rather than PDFs, so the corpus is auditable without redistributing copyrighted material. Includes TRG (Timing-Recovery-Grounded), a minimum reporting standard for real-time voice agent evaluation, with a fillable template and a compliance validator.

title: SILT Core v0.2: Semantic Architecture
abstract: SILT Core v0.2 is a semantic architecture for moments of encounter between participants and systems grounded in different legal, customary, cultural, private, institutional or technical orders. Its canonical seam is Source to Standing to Presentation to evaluation at the encounter. SILT enables relevant relational legitimacy to become mutually legible without requiring originating orders to collapse into a single ontology or surrender their own sources of authority. The v0.2 release includes the normative semantic architecture, a unified minimal semantic conformance suite spanning four base encounters and thirty adversarial variants, governance and licensing material, and an experimental non-normative mapping to Legal Context Protocol.Licensing is path-specific: narrative specification and documentation are licensed CC BY 4.0; machine-readable conformance artefacts, bindings, scripts, examples and reference code are licensed Apache License 2.0. See LICENSING.md in the archived release.

title: Experimental evaluation of compression algorithms for memory-constrained embedded systems
abstract: Introduction Embedded systems are constrained by limited flash memory, RAM (random access memory), and processing power, making efficient local data storage and transmission challenging. This study evaluates the suitability of several lossless compression algorithms for resource-constrained embedded platforms and assesses how data representation influences compression performance. Methods LZW, Heatshrink, LZ4, FastLZ, and Miniz were evaluated directly on an STM32U575ZI microcontroller (Arm Cortex-M33, 160 MHz). A 104,067-byte sensor dataset comprising repetitive time-series measurements of soil and ambient temperature, humidity, battery voltage, timestamps, and identifiers was used as the test workload. The dataset was stored in three formats: CSV (comma-separated values) (104,067 bytes), binary (33,576 bytes), and bit-packed binary (26,581 bytes). Compression ratio, execution time, and total application RAM consumption, including input and output buffers, were measured. Results Miniz achieved the highest compression efficiency, reducing the 33,576-byte binary dataset to 11,352 bytes (33.81% of the original size). The fastest compression was obtained with LZ4 configured with acceleration = 16, which compressed the bit-packed representation in 9.437 ms and produced a 25,692-byte output. Among configurations selected for minimum compressed output, FastLZ achieved the shortest execution time at 31.653 ms. When total RAM consumption was evaluated consistently, including all required buffers, LZ4 operating on the bit-packed representation required the least memory among the minimum-output configurations, consuming 58,496 bytes. Discussion The results demonstrate significant trade-offs between compression ratio, execution speed, and memory requirements in embedded environments. Data representation substantially influences compression effectiveness, with binary and bit-packed formats generally improving efficiency over CSV. The findings provide practical guidance for selecting compression algorithms in resource-constrained embedded systems, where minimizing storage, execution time, or memory usage may be prioritized depending on application requirements.

title: Resource-Effcient Quantum Beneš Networks
abstract: Abstract Distributing quantum states and entanglement between multiple pairs of nodes is a fundamental task in quantum communication and distributed quantum computing on large-scale quantum networks. In particular, the simultaneous distribution of quantum states or entanglement among multiple source-destination pairs (quantum k -pair communication task) is an emerging demand for scalable quantum networks. Here, we propose a quantum network architecture based on the Beneš switching topology that provides a universal switching framework for such pairwise communications. Our network architecture requires only O ( k log k ) pre-established entangled resources to accomplish the k -pair communication task, and offers advantages of non-blocking and low latency. We develop routing protocols for concurrent entanglement distribution and analyze their performance under ideal operating assumptions, while also discussing the effects of nonideal entanglement generation, quantum memory decoherence, photon loss, and finite Bell state measurement (BSM) success probability. The proposed framework requires local BSMs and entanglement swapping operations and is compatible in principle with quantum platforms supporting these capabilities. In particular, photonic implementations can benefit from mature photonic components and be compatible with existing telecommunications infrastructure.

title: Transfer learning guided by cultural distance enables effective cross cultural content adaptation
abstract: Artificial intelligence-driven multilingual text generation technology offers new approaches for cross-cultural content dissemination. However, existing models still struggle to effectively handle cross-cultural differences in value orientations, narrative conventions, and pragmatic preferences during content adaptation, which often leads to communication losses in the target culture. To address this problem, this paper proposes a transfer learning-driven cultural discount reduction network (TL-CDRNet). Built upon a pretrained multilingual encoder-decoder Transformer, the model incorporates a shared-private transfer adaptation module, a cultural distance guidance module, a transferability filtering module, and a transfer-feedback cultural discount optimization module, enabling synergistic optimization of cross-cultural knowledge transfer and target-cultural expression adaptation. Experiments are conducted on three tasks: film synopsis adaptation, tourism promotional text rewriting, and cultural creative/intangible cultural heritage product description adaptation. Results show that TL-CDRNet outperforms baseline methods in terms of BLEU, ROUGE-L, BERTScore, and semantic consistency, reducing the cultural discount score to 0.298 and increasing the cultural discount reduction rate to 43.7%. Moreover, the model exhibits satisfactory stability and generalization ability under low-resource and cross-domain conditions. This study demonstrates that transfer learning-based AI models can more effectively achieve cross-cultural content adaptation while preserving original semantics, offering a new technical pathway for intelligent text generation in cultural communication scenarios.

title: Zero-Shot Visualization: Exploring Text Corpora with User-Prompted Axes
abstract: We study the application of large language models (LLMs) to the visual exploration of textual corpora. We introduce zero-shot visualization (ZSV), a task in which users specify concepts in natural language and documents are mapped onto the corresponding concept axes for visualization. Building a ZSV system of practical value is non-trivial, as it requires choices at the intersection of feature functions, efficient implementation tradeoffs, and pre/post-processing decisions affecting visualization quality. To that end, we establish a benchmark that compares methods spanning embedding similarity, direct semantic judgments, and conditional likelihood estimation in this setting. Across multiple datasets and use cases we evaluate the properties of different scoring methods and design choices in terms of semantic faithfulness, score fidelity, and computational cost. Our results identify that scoring based on next-token probabilities offers the strongest practical trade-off among the evaluated methods. We further apply this approach to unlabeled corpora to examine its behavior in realistic exploratory settings. These experiments highlight additional design considerations, including the use of graded axes together with binary relevance filtering, and reveal a compositional sentiment bias in off-topic documents. Based on these findings, we provide practical guidelines for constructing end-to-end ZSV baselines.
